scores.accuracy_concern: Verify the MMSE bands and likelihood ratios against the Sessums abstract (cut-points are quoted differently in secondary sources); a high score lowers but does not rule out incapacity, especially with executive impairment.
scores.sharpen: Add that even a score above 24 does not rule out incapacity for a complex decision, linking to observed function.

scores.values_concern: Avoid shaming care staff; elderspeak is common and usually well meant, and the post should say so.
scores.accuracy_concern: Verify CHAT effect sizes and whether the fall in resistiveness (not only elderspeak) persisted at 3 months; Williams 2009 is observational sequence analysis in 20 residents, so 'more likely after' is association.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the ordinary-kindness framing so staff recognise their phrases without feeling accused, and give only verified CHAT figures.

scores.accuracy_concern: NICE SC1 wording on who attends the best-interests discussion must be quoted exactly; in Scotland the Mental Welfare Commission guide requires AWI authority (s47 certificate with a covert plan); the NICE and CQC pages were not openable, so a published paper or opened document is needed.
scores.sharpen: Give the Scottish route alongside NICE SC1 and keep 'stop the medicines not worth hiding' prominent.

scores.accuracy_concern: Baker J's wording in CC v KK must be quoted from the judgment, not paraphrased; it is a first-instance England and Wales judgment; Foulkes 2024 studied acquired brain injury, not older people.
scores.sharpen: Quote the judgment's words and add that the care home option must also be described honestly, including its own drawbacks.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check the AWI subsection (s16(5)) and include the 'attorney reasonably believes' limb in both jurisdictions; OPG guidance pages were not openable, so rely on statute text.
scores.sharpen: Add what to say if staff turn to the attorney first ('She can decide this; please ask her'), and keep the financial-powers footnote.

scores.accuracy_concern: Clayman 2005 is a cross-sectional US study of 93 patients, so companion behaviours are linked with, not shown to cause, patient involvement; 'clinicians turn to the companion' needs its own source.
scores.sharpen: State the association plainly and add one before-the-appointment step, such as agreeing with your parent which questions they want to ask themselves.

scores.values_concern: Make sure observed task failure is not used as a shortcut to override a person's choices.
scores.accuracy_concern: 'Frontal lobe paradox' is a loosely used, contested label and the listed sources are uncertain; the case law on 'executive capacity' needs a named judgment.
scores.sharpen: Source 'executive capacity' to a named Court of Protection judgment or the 39 Essex Chambers guidance note rather than the contested label, and keep the step of putting the observations to the person.

scores.accuracy_concern: The trials were not in older people specifically; 'no clear pattern' at very low certainty is an evidence gap, not evidence that teach-back fails; the NHS recommendation source is unidentified.
scores.sharpen: Add the older-patient angle (recall falls with age; teach-back as a check in decision conversations) and keep 'not shown' rather than 'does not work'.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Scotland paragraph must describe AWI correctly (incapacity is decision-specific under s1(6); s47 certificates are treatment-specific and time-limited); the claim that records drift into 'lacks capacity' as a label is an observation to phrase as a risk, not a finding.
scores.sharpen: Give the exact wording to write ('Lacks capacity to decide X; assessed by [role] on [date]; review when Y') and add the Scottish s47 equivalent.

scores.accuracy_concern: Flores 2012 error rates need verifying before any number is used; Karliner 2007 is not specific to older people; NHS England 2018 guidance applies to primary care commissioning in England.
scores.sharpen: Add the older-person angle (hearing loss alongside an interpreter; cognitive tests through interpreters) and verify any error-rate number.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Entitled to ask' overstates guidance: the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges recommends patient-addressed letters but this is not a legal right; the Moorfields figures (about 2 in 100 addressed to patients) come from one eye hospital and must not be generalised to all clinics.
scores.sharpen: Say you can ask for a letter written to you or a copy of the GP letter, keep the Moorfields figure labelled as one eye hospital, and add that you can say if you would rather letters did not come to your home.

scores.accuracy_concern: Evidence is one small within-couple comparison (18 couples), not randomised or long-term; 'cheap' and 'low-tech' are uncosted, and Talking Mats is a licensed resource that needs training, so naming it risks reading as endorsement.
scores.sharpen: Say how people get access (training, cost) in neutral terms and keep the 18-couple limitation in the caption.

scores.accuracy_concern: The BSL Acts recognise the language but do not themselves create a right to an interpreter; the duty comes from the Equality Act 2010 and, in England, the Accessible Information Standard; Emond 2015 and SignHealth details need verifying.
scores.sharpen: Retitle to avoid the 'X, not Y' shape and name the Equality Act as the basis for asking.

scores.accuracy_concern: The review covers studies from 2000 to about 2016; the 'most people over 80' prevalence figure must come from a primary US survey, not the review's introduction.
scores.sharpen: Add the date limitation and one bedside habit (ask 'Can you hear me clearly?' and use an amplifier before any decision conversation); consider moving to C20 if that category is short.

scores.values_concern: Avoid implying guilt for relatives who stayed quiet at a bedside, or false hope about understanding.
scores.accuracy_concern: The number of unresponsive patients was small and must be given; whether 'most' showed mismatch responses needs checking; brain responses to tones are not evidence of hearing words or understanding. Possible overlap with C19 candidates.
scores.sharpen: Give the exact number of unresponsive patients, keep the 'what it did not test' panel, and add that relatives who did not talk have not failed anyone.
Add a concrete example of the everyday decisions the person still makes after a finding about where to live, and the follow-up question 'What help will she get to make the others?'

scores.values_concern: Say clearly that relatives' knowledge of the person is essential, so families do not feel sidelined.
scores.accuracy_concern: GMC wording that relatives should not be given the impression they decide is unverified; Scotland's route (s47, consultation with any welfare attorney or guardian) differs; Wendler and Rid are mostly US studies.
scores.sharpen: Add the Scottish route and invite relatives to bring what the person said, in the person's own words.

scores.accuracy_concern: Scotland's position must be phrased carefully (no statute; advance directives must be taken into account under AWI principles and are likely to be treated as binding at common law, but untested); an advance decision can refuse but never demand treatment.
scores.sharpen: Write the Scottish paragraph carefully and add giving copies to the GP and family so the document is found when needed.

scores.accuracy_concern: For decisions carried out day after day (medicines, living at home), inability to retain can bear on using and weighing, so forgetting is not always irrelevant; the Code paragraph on memory aids needs checking.
scores.sharpen: Add one line that memory can matter for decisions that must be carried out repeatedly, and move the post to Teaching round or Ask this rather than Who gets left out.

scores.accuracy_concern: A DNACPR decision based on a clinical judgement that CPR would not work is not the recovered person's to reverse, though they can discuss it and seek a second opinion; the GMC wording is unverified; 'nobody routinely hands these back' is unsupported.
scores.sharpen: Separate decisions that return to the person (a stopped medicine, a care home referral) from resuscitation decisions, and phrase the hand-back gap as a question to ask rather than a finding.

scores.accuracy_concern: The studies are small and old (15 people in 1997; 18 couples in 2003); 'slow speech did not help on its own' must not become 'slow speech is wrong'; for people who are also hard of hearing, clear speech (often slower) helps, which C09-04 relies on.
scores.sharpen: State the sample sizes in the post and reconcile with hearing advice so the two posts do not contradict each other.

scores.values_concern: Could discourage families from talking about wishes; keep conversations encouraged alongside writing things down.
scores.accuracy_concern: Shalowitz 2006 used hypothetical scenarios in mostly US studies; some later structured advance care planning trials improved patient and surrogate agreement, so 'prior discussion did not improve accuracy' applies to the observational studies reviewed, not to structured planning.
scores.sharpen: Add that structured planning conversations improved agreement in some later trials, so the message is 'write it down and talk it through'.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Doing them changes the result for some people' is unsupported; Dupuis 2015 (sensory loss and MoCA scores) is uncertain and concerns cognitive tests, not capacity findings.
scores.sharpen: Cut the checklist to five or six items for phone legibility and support or remove the 'changes the result' claim.

scores.accuracy_concern: SAR thematic findings need exact wording from Preston-Shoot; Care Act and SARs are England-specific; the House of Lords report is from 2014; 'the case is often closed' is a generalisation.
scores.sharpen: Quote the SAR findings exactly and add the Scottish equivalent (Adult Support and Protection) so Scottish readers are included.

scores.accuracy_concern: Aphasia after stroke can coexist with cognitive impairment, so 'keep their judgement' must be 'may keep'; aphasia prevalence and Jayes 2026 survey details need verifying.
scores.sharpen: Change the opening to 'may keep their judgement' and give one action: ask the speech and language therapist before the capacity conversation.

scores.values_concern: Could be read as eroding the presumption of capacity; frame as considering capacity for significant decisions, not formally assessing everyone who agrees.
scores.accuracy_concern: 'People who agree are least likely to be checked' has no identified source; the Raymont recognition figure must be verified; 'consent forms signed by people unable to consent' is an inference; these inpatient samples include acute illness.
scores.sharpen: Replace the unsourced agreement claim with the verified recognition figure and say that the presumption of capacity still stands.

scores.accuracy_concern: Supporting studies are old and tiny (Picheny 1985, a handful of listeners; Sumby and Pollack 1954 in noise, not at night); 'raising the voice distorts speech' needs a named source; prevalence figures are US survey data.
scores.sharpen: Cut the laboratory studies to one sourced line, open with the four actions, and say that waking someone to put aids in is for conversations that need an answer.

scores.accuracy_concern: England only; the date and content of the revised standard are unverified; the link from unmet formats to missed appointments is asserted without a source; NHS England pages were not openable in this project.
scores.sharpen: Anchor the claim to the current published version of the standard and one published figure on unmet formats, and give the exact request wording ('Please send my letters in 20-point print, as recorded').

scores.values_concern: Frame the findings as legal and system gaps during extreme pandemic pressure, not as blame of ward staff or families.
scores.accuracy_concern: The count of unlawful moves and its denominator must be verified from the report; the review covers March to May 2020 only and practice may have changed; the report is on the Commission site, which may not be openable here.
scores.sharpen: Give the verified count with its denominator, say plainly that the review covered the first pandemic months, and end with the three questions at the care home door.

scores.accuracy_concern: Jayes 2020 is a small case series (4 of 8 unscreened patients), too thin for a headline; the 'social facade' source is unidentified; Sessums recognition figure overlaps C09-14 and C09-26.
scores.sharpen: Drop the case-series numbers from the headline and lead with the two-way statute point and one concrete pair of examples (a fluent person unable to weigh, a deaf person fully able).

scores.values_concern: Keep the criticism on commissioning conditions, not on care workers, and avoid implying a position on funding policy.
scores.accuracy_concern: NICE NG21 applies in England and its exact wording on visit length must be quoted; the prevalence of 15-minute visits has no identified published source; the link from short visits to loss of choice is argument, not a measured finding.
scores.sharpen: Quote the NG21 recommendation exactly, drop the 15-minute prevalence claim unless a published figure is found, and add what a family can ask the provider for.

scores.accuracy_concern: The review-trigger method is good practice drawn from guidance, not a tested intervention; the 2007 Department of Health guide is old and England-specific.
scores.sharpen: Address the older person directly ('If you choose to stay at home...'), show a worked trigger list, and say the method is good practice rather than trial-tested.

allocation_reason: All 32 candidates clear about 36 with no disqualifying flag and 22 score 44 or more; capacity and supported decision-making is absent from the earlier collection, so the category can take the maximum without repetition.
balance_note: The top 14 by score are practitioner-heavy (9 practitioner, 3 public: C09-11, C09-09, C09-02; 2 both: C09-22, C09-27), against a brief that asks this category to address older people directly. For a balanced 14, swap C09-20 (better placed in C20), C09-23 (no older-person angle) and one of C09-01 or C09-12 for public posts C09-15, C09-24 and C09-10 (or C09-16 or C09-29), giving roughly 6 practitioner, 6 public and 2 both. Avoid pairing C09-14 with C09-26 (both lean on Sessums 2011), C09-13 with C09-31, or C09-03 with C09-30. Most legal posts rest on the England and Wales Mental Capacity Act; every one needs an accurate Scottish line, and at least one Scotland-specific post (C09-06 or C09-22) should be included.
